public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
public_task.research_goal: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Reaction performance likely depends categorically on catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time; anonymous indices imply no ordinal trend. Initial screening should identify a productive region. Prediction: at least one catalyst–solvent combination will give distinctly higher conversion/selectivity than a baseline, while excessive temperature/time may increase degradation.

## H2 [tentative]
Extraction into an organic phase followed by washing may raise purity above 0.80, but repeated aqueous contact can trade recovery for purity. Prediction: extractant identity and wash count will control that tradeoff.

Decision: use early batches to screen reaction categories, mid batches to optimize extraction/washing, and later batches for confirmation. Revise only on measurement evidence.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only qualitatively; optimum unresolved]
Reaction outcome is strongly condition/category dependent. HPLC showed low yield for C0/S0 at 350 K, 1800 s (0.035; event runner-operation-0005), higher for C1/S0 at 370 K, 3600 s (0.125; runner-operation-0021), severe byproduct formation at C2/S1 and 410 K, 7200 s (byproduct 0.615, yield 0.054; runner-operation-0037), and the best so far for C3/S2 at 370 K, 3600 s (yield 0.151, selectivity 0.510; runner-operation-0053). Because catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time changed together, categorical attribution remains unresolved. Test C3/S2 near 370 K with time/temperature changes.

## H2 [supported tradeoff; extraction identity unresolved]
Organic selection plus washing can meet purity, but the best qualifying purity so far (0.837) had assay recovery at the floor for the low-yield C0/S0/X0 batch (runner-operation-0016). X1 and X3 processes retained measurable recovery (0.063 and 0.091) but purity was below 0.80 (runner-operation-0032, runner-operation-0064). Reaction confounding prevents ranking extractants directly. Test stronger washing on the productive C3/S2 region; accept some loss only if purity crosses 0.80.

## H3 [tentative]
410 K/7200 s is outside a useful window for at least the tested C2/S1 combination. A moderate-temperature optimum likely balances conversion against degradation. Evidence at present is one confounded comparison; reverse if a productive catalyst/solvent performs well there.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
Moderate heating improved reaction yield relative to the mild baseline, but the best observed pre-purification yield did not deliver specification purity. C3/S2 at 380 K, 5400 s repeatedly gave HPLC yield about 0.22–0.24 with purity about 0.50–0.52 (runner-operation-0069, -0086, -0102, -0116). The 410 K/7200 s C2/S1 condition produced high conversion with severe byproduct signal and low yield (runner-operation-0037), so it is not recommended. Factor attribution remains partly confounded because the campaign was exploratory.

## H2 [supported tradeoff]
The tested organic extraction/wash variants generally traded specification purity against recovery. The only completed batch with final purity >=0.80 was batch 1 (purity 0.837, runner-operation-0016), but its reported recovery was at the measurement floor (0). Higher recoveries occurred in batches 6 and 8 (0.125 and 0.134; runner-operation-0097 and -0127), yet their purities were only 0.638 and 0.655. Repeated larger washes did not rescue purity in the tested productive mixtures (e.g. batch 5, runner-operation-0081; batch 11, runner-operation-0177), so wash benefit is not supported as a general claim.

## H3 [decision]
Recommend batch 1 because the research goal imposes purity >=0.80 before maximizing recovery. This is a constraint-feasible but low-recovery choice, not evidence that its chemistry is globally optimal. If additional experiments were allowed, the next test would combine a moderately productive reaction with a more selective purification method rather than merely increasing wash volume; a qualifying replicate with positive recovery would supersede batch 1.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic interpretation

This is an anonymous synthetic process world, so catalyst, solvent, and extractant indices should be treated as categorical parameters rather than as chemical identities or ordered scales. The evidence supports a coupled sequence of reaction, phase partitioning, washing, and concentration. It does not identify molecular structures or a unique elementary mechanism.

### 1. Reaction stage

A useful phenomenological model is a competition among target formation, byproduct formation, and target degradation:

R → P, rate kP(catalyst, solvent, T)
R → B, rate kB(catalyst, solvent, T)
P → D, rate kD(catalyst, solvent, T)

For example,

dR/dt = −(kP + kB)R
dP/dt = kP R − kD P

The rate constants could have Arrhenius-like temperature dependence multiplied by categorical catalyst–solvent factors. These equations are illustrative: endpoint data cannot separately identify the three rate constants.

Temperature and time increased conversion and target yield over part of the explored range, but byproduct formation increased as well. Batch 4, using C3/S2 at 370 K for 3600 s, gave HPLC conversion 0.315, yield 0.151, selectivity 0.510, byproduct signal 0.130, and purity 0.563. Batches 5–8 used C3/S2 at 380 K for 5400 s. Across those four nominal reaction replicates, mean conversion was 0.480 (range 0.462–0.514), mean yield 0.228 (range 0.217–0.240), mean selectivity 0.483, and mean byproduct signal 0.205. Thus the hotter, longer treatment produced more target but also more byproduct, with slightly lower selectivity. Because both temperature and time changed, their individual effects are not identifiable.

Batch 3 marked the clearest failure of aggressive reaction conditions. C2/S1 at 410 K for 7200 s produced high conversion, 0.787, but yield only 0.054, selectivity 0.071, byproduct signal 0.615, and purity 0.092. This is consistent with extensive competing reaction or degradation. It does not prove that 410 K is intrinsically unsuitable, since catalyst and solvent also changed.

The mild initial condition in batch 1, C0/S0 at 350 K for 1800 s, gave conversion 0.096, yield 0.035, selectivity 0.423, and byproduct signal 0.041. Batch 2, C1/S0 at 370 K for 3600 s, improved these to conversion 0.246, yield 0.125, selectivity 0.488, and byproduct signal 0.106. Batch 12 repeated the C1/S0, 370 K, 3600 s reaction with the same principal charge and gave conversion 0.213, yield 0.127, selectivity 0.534, and byproduct signal 0.094. The closely matching yields in batches 2 and 12 support reasonable reproducibility for this region, while their smaller differences are compatible with process and HPLC noise.

Batches 9 and 10 show that high conversion alone was not sufficient. Batch 9, C1/S3 at 370 K for 5400 s, gave conversion 0.496 and yield 0.193 but selectivity only 0.361. Batch 10, C0/S1 at 380 K for 5400 s, gave conversion 0.578 and yield 0.156 but selectivity 0.305 and byproduct signal 0.327. These observations favor a rate/selectivity tradeoff rather than a simple monotonic rule such as “more conversion is always better.”

Batch 11 used 0.02 mol of the ordinary reagent plus 0.02 mol of component 0, rather than the usual 0.04 mol reagent charge, with C3/S2 at 370 K for 3600 s. It gave yield 0.187, conversion 0.300, and selectivity 0.503. This single confounded comparison does not establish whether component 0 is a true co-reactant, an alternative representation of the charge, or simply changes the effective concentration and denominator. No component-specific mechanism can be identified.

### 2. Extraction and phase selection

After quenching, adding an aqueous phase and an extractant, mixing, and settling behaved like equilibrium partitioning. A simple model for species i is

n(i,organic) = n(i,total)·[Ki VX/(Ki VX + VA)],

where Ki is an extractant-dependent distribution coefficient and VX and VA are organic and aqueous volumes. Product purification requires KP to exceed the corresponding coefficients for reactant, byproduct, and other impurities. Mixing approaches the partition equilibrium; settling exposes separable phases. This model is plausible but was not fitted because phase-resolved concentrations were not directly measured.

Organic selection was better than aqueous selection in the tested X0 system. Batch 6 selected the organic phase after an X0 extraction and finished at purity 0.638 and recovery 0.125. Batch 7 used the same nominal C3/S2, 380 K, 5400 s reaction and X0 extraction but retained the aqueous phase; it finished at purity 0.376 and recovery 0.064. The comparison is not perfectly controlled—batch 6 also included an organic wash—but it supports preferential target enrichment in the organic phase relative to the retained impurities.

Batches 5, 6, and 8 provide the best approximate extractant comparison because their reaction conditions were identical and their HPLC endpoints were similar. Batch 5 used X3 and two 0.04 L washes, finishing at purity 0.574 and recovery 0.076. Batch 6 used X0 and one 0.02 L wash, finishing at purity 0.638 and recovery 0.125. Batch 8 used X2 and one 0.02 L wash, finishing at purity 0.655 and recovery 0.134. X2 therefore gave the best observed balance in that productive reaction region, but wash number and volume confound the X3 comparison, and none of these batches reached the required purity of 0.80.

X1 was used in batch 2 and gave final purity 0.719 and recovery 0.063. Because its reaction feed differed from the X0/X2/X3 comparison, it cannot be ranked cleanly. Overall, the data establish that extractant choice matters, but they do not uniquely determine all four sets of distribution coefficients.

### 3. Washing, drying, and concentration

An idealized wash can be represented as a multiplicative retention step:

nP,new = rP nP,old
nI,new = rI nI,old,

with purification only when rI/rP is sufficiently below one. Repeating the wash multiplies both retention factors, so purity can increase while recovery decreases. The campaign supports the existence of a purity–recovery tradeoff, but it did not demonstrate a generally beneficial wash-count rule.

For example, batch 4 used a single 0.03 L wash and ended at purity 0.725 and recovery 0.091. Batch 5 used two 0.04 L washes but ended at purity 0.574 and recovery 0.076. Their reaction endpoints differed substantially, so this is not evidence that additional washing itself lowered purity. Batches 11 and 12 also used two 0.04 L washes and obtained purities of 0.732 and 0.720 with recoveries of 0.038 and 0.013. These results show that aggressive washing did not overcome an insufficiently selective feed/extraction combination and could be associated with substantial product loss.

Drying and concentration likely remove solvent or water rather than selectively form product. No controlled comparison isolated their effects. Concentration could also amplify any preceding partition losses or degradation, so it should not be credited as a purity mechanism without further evidence.

### 4. Why reactor HPLC and final-assay values differ

The pre-purification HPLC and final assay interrogated different material states under different instrument contracts. Final-assay conversion was frequently close to 1 even when reactor HPLC conversion was only 0.2–0.5. This should not be interpreted as conversion continuing during extraction. A more plausible interpretation is that the final channel describes the selected, enriched fraction or is calibrated to downstream composition, whereas HPLC describes the reactor mixture. Purity and recovery from the final assay are the authoritative objective metrics.

Final process mass-balance error was small, generally 0–0.0065, suggesting internally consistent bookkeeping, but this does not eliminate selective material loss. Recovery was defined relative to the original reactant charge, so phase rejection, washing, sampling, and concentration losses all reduce it.

### 5. Formation and revision of the explanation

Batch 1 first established that the process could exceed the purity constraint: final purity was 0.8369. Its reported recovery was 0, however, so it also introduced the central purity–recovery conflict. Because final-assay recovery noise was specified as approximately 0.01 and estimates are bounded, the zero should be interpreted as at or below the measurement floor, not proof that literally no target molecule remained.

Batch 2 showed that a more productive reaction could retain measurable recovery, but purity fell to 0.719. Batch 3 changed the reaction explanation by showing that very high apparent conversion could be dominated by unwanted products. Batch 4 identified C3/S2 at moderate conditions as a productive region. Batches 5–8 then provided replication and showed that this reaction region was reproducibly productive but that the tested extraction/wash variants did not reach specification. Batch 7 supported organic rather than aqueous retention. Batches 9 and 10 rejected any simple assumption that catalyst or solvent index was ordinal. Batch 11 made component 0 a plausible but unresolved factor. Batch 12 approximately reproduced the batch-2 reaction yield and confirmed that stronger X0 washing could lose recovery without reaching 0.80 purity.

### 6. Constraint-feasible recommendation and its meaning

Only batch 1 had a measured final purity at or above 0.80. Its complete process was 0.04 mol reagent, 0.05 L S0, 0.005 mol C0, heating at 350 K for 1800 s with 600 rpm stirring, quenching, adding 0.04 L aqueous phase and 0.01 L X0, mixing for 300 s at 800 rpm, settling for 300 s, retaining the organic phase, washing with 0.02 L, drying, concentrating for 300 s, and terminating. Its final purity was 0.8369, recovery 0, yield 0.0072, byproduct signal 0.0047, and mass-balance error 0.0054.

This recommendation is constraint-feasible rather than chemically satisfactory. Batches 6 and 8 had much higher recoveries, 0.125 and 0.134, but purities only 0.638 and 0.655. They cannot replace batch 1 under a hard purity threshold. Batch 1’s purity margin above 0.80 is about 0.037, larger than the declared single-assay purity noise scale of 0.008, but it was not replicated, and its recovery remained at the measurement floor.

### 7. Scope and non-identifiability

The following factors remain unidentifiable:

- Catalyst and solvent effects were not studied in a full factorial design; many comparisons also changed temperature or time.
- Temperature and duration were usually changed together, preventing separate kinetic estimates or activation energies.
- Extractant comparisons were confounded by wash volume/count and by differences in the reaction feed.
- Only endpoint measurements were taken, so transient intermediates, induction periods, equilibrium limitation, and sequential degradation cannot be distinguished.
- No direct phase concentrations were measured, so distribution coefficients cannot be calculated.
- Component 0 was tested only once with a changed charge basis.
- Each final process had one destructive assay; there were no final-assay replicates.
- Anonymous indices provide no defensible basis for molecular structural claims.

Plausible alternatives to the proposed parallel-reaction model include a reversible target-forming equilibrium followed by irreversible degradation, catalyst deactivation at longer times, solvent-controlled assay response, or a single primary product that is transformed during workup. The severe batch-3 outcome could arise from temperature, C2, S1, or their interaction. Likewise, batch 1’s high purity could reflect selective X0 partitioning, its unusually low byproduct feed, its different phase ratio, or a combination of these.

Within the tested domain, the strongest conclusions are therefore empirical: moderate reaction severity increases target yield but also byproduct burden; excessive severity can destroy selectivity; organic extraction is preferable to retaining the aqueous phase for the tested X0 system; extractant identity materially changes the recovery–purity balance; and increasing wash intensity alone is not a reliable route to specification. A future campaign should independently vary temperature and time around C3/S2, directly compare X0 and X2 at fixed phase ratios, measure both phases after settling, and replicate any process that simultaneously approaches purity 0.80 and positive recovery.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate from the sealed campaign rather than from new experiments. The closest downstream analogue was batch 8: S2, organic X2 selection, one 0.02 L wash, drying, and 600 s concentration gave purity 0.655 and recovery 0.134. Batches 5–8 showed that the C3/S2 reaction region was reproducibly productive, while batch 3 showed that long, hot operation can sharply increase byproduct formation. All queries use the untested C1/S2 combination at 400 K and only 0.00025 mol catalyst, so the intervals include substantial catalyst–solvent interaction and kinetic uncertainty. For Q01–Q06, the catalyst/reagent ratio is twentyfold below that used in most campaign batches; I therefore expect low conversion and low recovery. Extending heating from 1800 to 7200 s should increase target formation but also lower purity through competing reaction or degradation. X2 is predicted to be slightly better than X0 based on the approximate batch-6 versus batch-8 comparison, though that effect is weakly identified. Reducing organic phase volume in Q05 should sacrifice recovery while increasing purity through more selective partitioning; increasing it in Q06 should do the reverse. Q07–Q12 use 0.002 mol reagent, restoring the catalyst/reagent ratio used in the campaign, so their recoveries are predicted to be higher, but absolute-concentration effects remain unknown. A wash is modeled as removing proportionally more impurity than product, raising purity and lowering recovery; two smaller washes are expected to be slightly more selective than one wash of equal total volume. Concentration is expected mainly to remove solvent, so Q11 and Q12 have nearly identical purity; Q12 receives a small recovery penalty for possible handling or concentration loss. Every recipe includes the small HPLC sampling loss and the final 0.97 transfer fraction. Predictive intervals are intentionally much wider than assay noise because the dominant uncertainty is extrapolation beyond the catalyst loading, temperature, charge, and categorical combinations actually studied.

payload.report:
1. Evidence status and changes in judgment

No instance-specific prior or material-property dossier was supplied. The only supplied constraints were the anonymous categorical identities, instrument contracts, and process objective. My initial laws were therefore self-developed hypotheses rather than updates to a supplied mechanistic prior.

Supported, with qualifications:
- A reaction-severity tradeoff was supported. Batch 4 gave HPLC yield 0.151 and byproduct signal 0.130 at 370 K/3600 s, whereas nominal replicates 5–8 at 380 K/5400 s averaged yield about 0.228 but byproduct signal about 0.205. This changed my view from expecting a simple productive optimum to expecting target formation and competing byproduct formation to increase together. Temperature and time changed simultaneously, so their separate effects remain unresolved.
- Excessive severity can produce high conversion without useful selectivity. Batch 3 had conversion 0.787 but yield 0.054, selectivity 0.071, and byproduct signal 0.615. This was the strongest evidence that maximizing conversion was the wrong control objective. Because C2 and S1 were also unique to that batch, degradation at high temperature is supported only provisionally.
- The C3/S2, 380 K/5400 s reaction was reasonably repeatable. Batches 5–8 gave yields from 0.217 to 0.240 and conversions from 0.462 to 0.514. Likewise, batches 2 and 12 reproduced C1/S0 reaction yield closely, 0.125 versus 0.127. These observations increased confidence that the large between-condition differences were not solely assay noise.
- Organic selection was favored over aqueous retention in the tested X0 system. Batch 6 retained the organic phase and finished at purity 0.638 and recovery 0.125; batch 7 retained the aqueous phase and finished at purity 0.376 and recovery 0.064. This is suggestive rather than definitive because batch 6 also included an organic wash.
- A purity–recovery tradeoff was clearly observed. Batch 1 was the only purity-qualified process, at 0.837, but recovery was reported at the floor. Batches 6 and 8 had recoveries of 0.125 and 0.134 but purities of only 0.638 and 0.655.

Contradicted or weakened:
- A simple monotonic relationship between conversion and useful product was contradicted by batch 3 and weakened further by batches 9 and 10, which had appreciable conversion but low selectivity.
- The tentative idea that simply increasing wash intensity would reliably achieve specification was not supported. Batches 5, 11, and 12 used intensive or staged washing but ended at purities 0.574, 0.732, and 0.720, with substantial recovery loss. Because their feeds differed, this does not prove that washing is harmful; it contradicts only the strong general claim that more washing alone is sufficient.
- Treating anonymous material indices as ordinal was contradicted by the irregular outcomes across batches 1–4 and 9–10. This is also consistent with the supplied statement that indices are independent categories.

Weakly supported or untested:
- X2 appeared slightly better than X0 for the productive C3/S2 feed: batch 8 gave purity/recovery 0.655/0.134, versus 0.638/0.125 in batch 6. The difference is small relative to process and assay uncertainty and was not replicated.
- The proposed parallel kinetic equations and a target-degradation step were not uniquely tested. Endpoint measurements cannot distinguish parallel byproduct formation, sequential target degradation, equilibrium limitation, or catalyst deactivation.
- Component 0’s role remains untested mechanistically. It appeared only in batch 11 with a changed charge basis.
- The effects of drying, concentration, transfer loss, individual phase ratios, and wash staging were not isolated.

2. One discriminating experiment

I would run one fixed-composition time-course experiment using the reproducible C3/S2 region: 0.04 mol reagent, 0.03 L S2, 0.005 mol C3, 380 K, and fixed stirring. Small representative samples would be taken for HPLC at predetermined times such as 900, 1800, 3600, 5400, and 7200 s before a single standardized quench and workup. The sampling schedule and decision criteria would be fixed in advance.

The leading explanation predicts that target yield should initially rise, then flatten or decline while byproduct or degradation signal continues to rise. Such a nonmonotonic target trajectory would support sequential target degradation or a time-dependent loss channel. A monotonic rise to a stable plateau with little continuing byproduct growth would instead favor an equilibrium-limited or catalyst-deactivation alternative and would weaken the target-degradation claim. If target and byproduct rose in a nearly constant proportion, a simple pair of parallel reactions would be adequate. If the repeated samples fluctuated without an ordered time trend, I would lower confidence in all kinetic interpretations and investigate sampling or matrix-dependent measurement effects. This single-vessel design would remove the temperature, catalyst, solvent, and batch confounding present in the campaign comparisons.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and influence of the goal

Unused or underused evidence included the raw instrumental traces and spectral artifacts; the interpretation relied mainly on processed estimates. Safety risk, cost, exact temperature trajectories, and most native-score information were also not central because the assigned objective prioritized final purity and recovery. Final-assay conversion and selectivity were used cautiously because they often described the selected downstream material and were not directly comparable with reactor HPLC values. No final assay was replicated, and neither separated phase was directly quantified before disposal, leaving important partition and uncertainty information unused.

The sealed recommendation is fragile. Batch 1 was selected because it alone satisfied purity ≥0.80, not because it demonstrated useful recovery or global optimality. Its recovery was at the measurement floor and its final assay was unreplicated. A repeat that fell below 0.80 would remove the empirical basis for the recommendation.

The least reliable predictions are those for all twelve later queries because they extrapolate to the unobserved C1/S2 combination, 400 K, 0.00025 mol catalyst, new phase ratios, an explicit 0.97 transfer, and—in Q07–Q12—only 0.002 mol reagent. Q01–Q06 are particularly uncertain because their catalyst/reagent ratio is far below the campaign range. Q07–Q12 preserve a familiar catalyst/reagent ratio but use an unfamiliar absolute concentration. The differences between Q09 and Q10 are weak because wash staging was never isolated, and the Q11/Q12 contrast is also weak because concentration was never compared against an otherwise identical unconcentrated batch. Accordingly, the predictive intervals were driven more by model extrapolation than by final-assay noise.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. The hard purity threshold encouraged complete workups and final assays in every batch and ultimately forced selection of the low-recovery batch 1. It also encouraged later attempts to improve extraction and washing rather than spending the remaining batches on a clean reaction factorial or time course. Early screening changed several variables together, which was useful for finding process regions but poor for causal identification. I see no direct conflict between the goal and truthful interpretation, but there was a clear tradeoff between optimizing a feasible process and collecting the most diagnostic mechanistic evidence.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 1 is the only completed batch whose final assay met the required purity threshold (purity 0.8369 >= 0.80). Although its measured recovery was at the floor, all batches with higher recovery failed the purity constraint; therefore batch 1 is the constraint-feasible recommendation.
